tool.name: ASP.NET Core
tool.tagline: Microsoft's fast, cross-platform framework for web APIs and services in C#
tool.description: ASP.NET Core is the open-source, cross-platform web framework of .NET for building HTTP APIs, web apps and real-time services in C#. It combines minimal APIs or MVC controllers with built-in dependency injection, configuration, logging, authentication and a very fast web server, Kestrel. It is a top choice for enterprise backends and cloud services, especially on Azure.

concepts.name: Your first ASP.NET Core app
concepts.summary: Create a web app with dotnet new web, understand Program.cs, the builder and the app, and run it with Kestrel.
concepts.why: Every ASP.NET Core service starts from this same small Program.cs structure.
concepts.body:
Create an app with `dotnet new web -o Api` (an empty app) or `dotnet new webapi` (with OpenAPI and a sample endpoint), then `dotnet run` or `dotnet watch` for hot reload. The app listens on the URLs from `Properties/launchSettings.json`, such as `http://localhost:5000`.

`Program.cs` has two phases:

- **Build**: `var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);` sets up configuration (appsettings.json, environment variables, command line), logging and the **dependency injection** container. You register services on `builder.Services`.
- **Run**: `var app = builder.Build();` creates the app. You add **middleware** (`app.UseX()`) and **endpoints** (`app.MapGet(...)`), then `app.Run()` starts the web server and blocks until shutdown.

The server is **Kestrel**, a cross-platform, high-performance HTTP server built into the framework. In production it can face the internet directly or sit behind a reverse proxy such as Nginx, IIS or a cloud load balancer.

The project uses the `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web` SDK, which references the whole ASP.NET Core shared framework, so no extra packages are needed for routing, JSON, DI, logging or configuration.

The **environment** (`ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT`: Development, Staging, Production) changes behavior such as detailed error pages and which appsettings file is loaded; check it with `app.Environment.IsDevelopment()`.
takeaways: CreateBuilder sets up config, logging and DI; Build creates the app
Register services before Build, add middleware and endpoints after
Kestrel is the built-in web server
ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT selects Development/Production behavior
pitfalls: Trying to register services on builder.Services after builder.Build() has been called.

quiz.q: Where do you register services such as a database context?
quiz.explain: The DI container is built by builder.Build(), so registrations must happen before it.

concepts.name: Routing and minimal API endpoints
concepts.summary: Map HTTP methods and URL patterns to handlers with MapGet, MapPost and friends, using route parameters and constraints.
concepts.why: Routes are the public surface of your API; designing and matching them correctly is step one.
concepts.body:
**Minimal APIs** map a route pattern and HTTP method directly to a handler, usually a lambda:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/todos/{id}", (int id) => ...);
```

There is a method per verb: `MapGet`, `MapPost`, `MapPut`, `MapPatch`, `MapDelete`, plus `MapMethods` for others. The handler can also be a method group (`app.MapGet("/x", Handlers.GetX)`), which keeps `Program.cs` short as the app grows.

Route templates:

- `{id}` captures a segment; a handler parameter with the same name receives it, converted to its type. A non-convertible value gives a 400 (for minimal APIs) rather than calling the handler.
- **Constraints** restrict matches: `{id:int}`, `{slug:alpha}`, `{n:min(1)}`, `{code:length(3)}`, `{date:datetime}`. With a constraint, `/todos/abc` doesn't match at all (404) so another route can take it.
- Optional `{id?}`, defaults `{page=1}`, and catch-all `{*path}`.

Routing picks the **most specific** matching endpoint regardless of declaration order: a literal segment like `/todos/today` beats `/todos/{id}`. Ambiguous matches raise an exception at request time.

Name endpoints with `.WithName("GetTodo")` so you can generate links to them, and use **route groups** (`app.MapGroup("/todos")`, Advanced level) to share prefixes and settings. Keep handlers thin: they should parse input, call a service and shape the response.
takeaways: MapGet/MapPost/... bind a verb and a route template to a handler
{name} segments bind to same-named handler parameters
Constraints like {id:int} make non-matching URLs fall through to 404
The most specific route wins, not the first declared
pitfalls: Relying on declaration order to pick between overlapping routes; ASP.NET Core ranks by specificity instead.

quiz.q: With routes /items/{id:int} and no other match, what does GET /items/abc return?
quiz.explain: The int constraint prevents the route from matching, so no endpoint is found.

concepts.name: Binding request data
concepts.summary: Get route values, query strings, headers, JSON bodies and services into handler parameters.
concepts.why: Correct binding gives you typed, validated input instead of parsing HttpContext by hand.
concepts.body:
Minimal API handlers declare what they need as parameters, and ASP.NET Core **binds** each one from the request. The rules, roughly in order:

- Explicit attributes win: `[FromRoute]`, `[FromQuery]`, `[FromHeader(Name = "X-Api-Key")]`, `[FromBody]`, `[FromForm]`, `[FromServices]`.
- Special types are injected directly: `HttpContext`, `HttpRequest`, `HttpResponse`, `CancellationToken` (canceled when the client disconnects), `ClaimsPrincipal`.
- A parameter whose name matches a route parameter binds from the route.
- Simple types (`int`, `string`, `Guid`, `DateTime`, enums, anything with `TryParse`) otherwise bind from the **query string**. Arrays like `int[] ids` bind from repeated keys `?ids=1&ids=2`.
- Types registered in DI bind from services.
- Any other complex type binds from the **JSON body** using `System.Text.Json` (camelCase by default). Only one body parameter is allowed.

Nullability matters: `string? q` or a default value (`int page = 1`) makes a query parameter optional; a non-nullable one that is missing produces a **400**.

`[AsParameters]` groups many parameters into one record or class, keeping handler signatures tidy.

Records are a natural fit for request bodies: `record CreateTodo(string Title, DateOnly? Due);`. Don't bind directly to database entities; use separate request models so clients can't set fields like `Id` or `IsAdmin`.
takeaways: Route names bind from the route, simple types from the query, complex types from the JSON body
Nullable or defaulted parameters are optional; missing required ones give 400
Use [FromHeader], [FromQuery] etc. to be explicit
Bind to request records, not database entities
pitfalls: Declaring two complex-type parameters and expecting both to come from the body.

quiz.q: For app.MapGet("/items", (int page) => ...), what does GET /items (no query string) return?
options: The handler runs with page = null
quiz.explain: page is a required non-nullable parameter, so missing input fails binding with 400.

concepts.name: Responses and status codes
concepts.summary: Return JSON, status codes and headers using plain objects, Results and TypedResults.
concepts.why: Clients depend on correct status codes and response shapes; this is your API contract.
concepts.body:
What a handler returns becomes the response:

- A `string` is written as `text/plain` with 200.
- Any other object (record, list, anonymous type) is serialized to **JSON** with 200.
- An `IResult` takes full control: status code, headers and body.

The `Results` and `TypedResults` static classes create IResults: `Ok(value)`, `Created(uri, value)`, `NoContent()`, `BadRequest(error)`, `NotFound()`, `Conflict()`, `Problem(...)`, `ValidationProblem(errors)`, `Unauthorized()`, `Forbid()`, `Redirect(url)`, `File(bytes, contentType)`, `Stream(...)`, `StatusCode(429)`.

Prefer **TypedResults**: they return concrete types like `Ok<Todo>`, so the handler's return type documents its outcomes and OpenAPI can describe them automatically. When a handler can produce several outcomes, declare a union return type:

```csharp
static Results<Ok<Todo>, NotFound> Get(int id) => ...
```

Each branch returns a different TypedResult, and the compiler checks that only the declared results are used.

Async handlers return `Task<T>` and work the same way. Use proper semantics: 201 with a Location header for creation, 204 for successful deletes without a body, 404 for missing resources, 400/422 for invalid input, 409 for conflicts.

JSON options (naming policy, enum as strings) are configured with `builder.Services.ConfigureHttpJsonOptions(o => ...)`.
takeaways: Objects become JSON, strings become text/plain
Return IResult for status codes and headers
TypedResults + Results<A, B> make outcomes explicit and documentable
Use the right status code for each outcome

quiz.q: Why prefer TypedResults.Ok(todo) over Results.Ok(todo)?
options: Its concrete return type documents the outcome for the compiler and OpenAPI
quiz.explain: TypedResults return specific types such as Ok<Todo>, which carry metadata about the response.

concepts.name: Dependency injection
concepts.summary: Register services with singleton, scoped and transient lifetimes and receive them in handlers and constructors.
concepts.why: DI is the backbone of every ASP.NET Core app: databases, HTTP clients, loggers and your own services flow through it.
concepts.body:
ASP.NET Core has a built-in **dependency injection** container. You register services on `builder.Services`, typically as an interface plus implementation, and the framework constructs them and passes them wherever they're needed: endpoint handler parameters, controller constructors, middleware, other services.

Lifetimes:

- **Singleton** (`AddSingleton`): one instance for the whole app. Must be thread-safe. Good for caches, configuration wrappers, `HttpClient` factories.
- **Scoped** (`AddScoped`): one instance per HTTP request. The default for EF Core `DbContext` and unit-of-work style services.
- **Transient** (`AddTransient`): a new instance every time it's requested. For lightweight, stateless services.

The container resolves constructor parameters recursively, so a service can depend on other services. Prefer constructor injection; avoid calling `IServiceProvider.GetService` yourself (the service locator anti-pattern).

The classic bug is a **captive dependency**: a singleton that takes a scoped service in its constructor keeps one instance of it forever, sharing a `DbContext` across requests. In Development the container validates scopes and throws on startup for this.

Other features: `TryAdd*` to avoid duplicate registrations, **keyed services** (`AddKeyedSingleton<IStore, S3Store>("s3")` with `[FromKeyedServices("s3")]`), and open generics (`AddScoped(typeof(IRepo<>), typeof(Repo<>))`). Libraries expose `AddX()` extension methods that register their services in one call.
takeaways: Register on builder.Services; the container builds and injects instances
Singleton = app, Scoped = request, Transient = every resolve
Never inject scoped services into singletons (captive dependency)
Prefer constructor injection over resolving from IServiceProvider
pitfalls: Registering a DbContext-using service as a singleton, sharing one non-thread-safe context across requests.

quiz.q: A singleton service takes a scoped service in its constructor. What's the problem?
options: None, the container creates a new scoped instance per call
The scoped instance is captured and lives as long as the singleton
quiz.explain: The singleton is created once, so it holds the first scoped instance forever: a captive dependency.

concepts.name: Configuration and options
concepts.summary: Read settings from appsettings.json, environment variables and secrets, and bind them to typed options classes.
concepts.why: Every deployed service needs environment-specific settings without code changes or committed secrets.
concepts.body:
`WebApplication.CreateBuilder` loads configuration from several **providers**, later ones overriding earlier ones:

1. `appsettings.json`
2. `appsettings.{Environment}.json` (e.g. `appsettings.Development.json`)
3. **User secrets** (Development only, `dotnet user-secrets set "Db:Password" "x"`)
4. **Environment variables**
5. Command-line arguments

Keys are hierarchical with `:` separators (`ConnectionStrings:Main`). In environment variables, use a double underscore instead: `Smtp__Host=mail.local` maps to `Smtp:Host`. This makes containers and cloud platforms easy to configure.

Read values directly with `builder.Configuration["Smtp:Host"]` or `GetConnectionString("Main")`, but prefer the **options pattern**: a plain class bound to a section.

```csharp
builder.Services.Configure<SmtpOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Smtp"));
```

Then inject `IOptions<SmtpOptions>` (read once, singleton), `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` (re-read per request, scoped) or `IOptionsMonitor<T>` (live updates with change notifications).

Validate options at startup so bad configuration fails fast: `AddOptions<SmtpOptions>().BindConfiguration("Smtp").ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart();`.

Never commit secrets to appsettings.json. Use user secrets locally and environment variables, Azure Key Vault or another secret store in production.
takeaways: Later providers override earlier ones: JSON, env-specific JSON, secrets, env vars, command line
Use __ in environment variable names for nested keys
Bind sections to classes with the options pattern
Validate options on start; keep secrets out of source control

quiz.q: Which environment variable sets the configuration key Logging:LogLevel:Default?
quiz.explain: A double underscore stands in for the : separator in environment variable names.

concepts.name: The middleware pipeline
concepts.summary: Understand how requests flow through ordered middleware, write inline middleware and place built-in ones correctly.
concepts.why: Exception handling, HTTPS, CORS, auth and static files are all middleware; order bugs are common and subtle.
takeaways: Middleware runs in registration order, then in reverse on the way out
Call next to continue; skip it to short-circuit
Exception handler first, authentication before authorization
Headers can't change after the response has started
pitfalls: Registering UseAuthorization before UseAuthentication, so the user is never authenticated when policies run.

quiz.q: Why is UseExceptionHandler usually registered first?
options: It is required to be first by the compiler
It can only catch exceptions thrown by middleware registered after it
quiz.explain: Middleware wraps the components added after it, so the earliest one sees all later exceptions.

concepts.name: MVC controllers for APIs
concepts.summary: Build APIs with [ApiController] classes, attribute routing, ActionResult<T> and automatic model validation.
concepts.why: Many existing codebases and teams use controllers; you need to read and write both styles.
concepts.body:
Controllers are the classic alternative to minimal APIs. A controller is a class deriving from `ControllerBase`, with **action methods** mapped by attributes:

```csharp
[ApiController]
[Route("api/[controller]")]
public class TodosController(ITodoStore store) : ControllerBase
```

- `[HttpGet("{id}")]`, `[HttpPost]`, `[HttpPut]`, `[HttpDelete]` map actions; `[controller]` is replaced with the class name without the `Controller` suffix.
- Return `ActionResult<T>`: either a `T` (serialized with 200) or helper results like `NotFound()`, `CreatedAtAction(...)`, `NoContent()`.
- Dependencies arrive via the constructor (a primary constructor is concise).

`[ApiController]` adds conventions: complex parameters bind from the body without `[FromBody]`, and an invalid model (failed DataAnnotations such as `[Required]`, `[Range]`, or a bad JSON body) automatically returns a **400 ValidationProblemDetails** before the action runs.

Register with `builder.Services.AddControllers()` and `app.MapControllers()`. Controllers and minimal APIs can coexist in one app.

Which to choose? Minimal APIs are leaner, faster to start and support Native AOT; controllers offer a structured convention with filters, model binding providers and familiar organization for large teams. New projects increasingly use minimal APIs organized with route groups and extension methods, but the concepts (routing, binding, results, DI) are the same.
takeaways: Controllers derive from ControllerBase and use attribute routing
ActionResult<T> returns either T or a status result
[ApiController] infers body binding and returns 400 on invalid models
AddControllers + MapControllers wire them up

quiz.q: What does [ApiController] do when a required property is missing from the JSON body?
options: Returns 400 with validation problem details before the action runs
quiz.explain: Automatic model validation short-circuits invalid requests with a ValidationProblemDetails response.

concepts.name: Data access with EF Core
concepts.summary: Map classes to database tables with Entity Framework Core: DbContext, migrations, LINQ queries and saving changes.
concepts.why: EF Core is the default way .NET services talk to relational databases.
concepts.body:
**Entity Framework Core** is .NET's object-relational mapper. You describe the model as classes, and EF Core translates LINQ queries to SQL and tracks changes to write back.

- Install a provider package, e.g. `Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL` or `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite`.
- Create a `DbContext` with a `DbSet<T>` per table.
- Register it: `builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDb>(o => o.UseNpgsql(connString))`. Contexts are **scoped**: one per request, not thread-safe.

**Migrations** evolve the schema: `dotnet ef migrations add Initial` generates C# code from model changes; `dotnet ef database update` applies it (in production, prefer generating an idempotent SQL script with `dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent`).

Querying uses LINQ on `IQueryable`, translated to SQL when you materialize with `ToListAsync`, `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, `CountAsync`. Write filters and projections **before** materializing so they run in the database. `Select` into DTOs to fetch only needed columns. `AsNoTracking()` speeds up read-only queries.

Saving: add, modify or remove tracked entities, then `await db.SaveChangesAsync()`, which runs all changes in one transaction. For bulk updates without loading entities use `ExecuteUpdateAsync` / `ExecuteDeleteAsync`.

Load related data explicitly with `Include(o => o.Items)`; lazy loading is off by default, which avoids hidden N+1 queries.
takeaways: DbContext + DbSet<T> model the database; register it scoped with AddDbContext
Migrations generate and apply schema changes
Filter and project before ToListAsync so work happens in SQL
SaveChangesAsync writes tracked changes in one transaction
pitfalls: Calling ToList() early and filtering in memory, loading whole tables.

quiz.q: Why must a DbContext not be registered as a singleton?
options: It can't be constructed by DI
It would use a different database
It isn't thread-safe and its change tracker would grow across all requests
quiz.explain: A DbContext is a short-lived unit of work; sharing one across concurrent requests corrupts its state.

concepts.name: Validation and error handling
concepts.summary: Validate input with data annotations, and return consistent ProblemDetails for errors and exceptions.
concepts.why: Clients need predictable error responses, and unhandled exceptions must never leak stack traces.
concepts.body:
**Validation.** ASP.NET Core 10 adds built-in validation for minimal APIs: call `builder.Services.AddValidation()` and annotate request types with DataAnnotations (`[Required]`, `[Range]`, `[StringLength]`, `[EmailAddress]`, `[RegularExpression]`). Invalid input gets a **400** with a `ValidationProblemDetails` body listing errors per field, before your handler runs. Controllers with `[ApiController]` have done this for a long time. For complex rules, implement `IValidatableObject` or use a library such as FluentValidation.

**Problem details** (RFC 9457) is the standard JSON error shape: `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance`, plus extensions. `builder.Services.AddProblemDetails()` makes the framework use it for error responses, and `TypedResults.Problem(...)` / `ValidationProblem(...)` let you return it yourself.

**Exceptions.** Register `app.UseExceptionHandler()` early in the pipeline so unhandled exceptions become a 500 problem response instead of a raw stack trace. In Development, the developer exception page shows details. To map specific exceptions to status codes, implement `IExceptionHandler` and register it with `AddExceptionHandler<T>()`; return `true` from `TryHandleAsync` when you've written the response.

`app.UseStatusCodePages()` adds bodies to empty 4xx/5xx responses (such as a 404 from routing).

Throwing exceptions for expected outcomes (not found, validation) is costly and hides control flow; return results for those and reserve exceptions for the unexpected.
takeaways: AddValidation + DataAnnotations validate minimal API input automatically (.NET 10)
ProblemDetails is the standard error body; enable it with AddProblemDetails
UseExceptionHandler turns unhandled exceptions into safe 500 responses
Return results for expected failures; keep exceptions exceptional
pitfalls: Returning exception messages or stack traces to clients in production.

quiz.q: What does UseExceptionHandler with AddProblemDetails return for an unhandled exception in Production?
options: A 500 response with a generic problem details body
quiz.explain: It catches the exception and writes a generic 500 problem details response without internal details.

concepts.name: Logging
concepts.summary: Write structured logs with ILogger<T>, message templates and log levels, and configure them per category.
concepts.why: Logs are your main window into production behavior and incidents.
concepts.body:
ASP.NET Core ships with `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging`. Inject `ILogger<T>` (the category is the type name) and call `LogInformation`, `LogWarning`, `LogError` and friends.

Use **message templates**, not string interpolation:

```csharp
logger.LogInformation("Order {OrderId} shipped to {City}", order.Id, city);
```

The named placeholders become structured properties that log backends (Seq, Elasticsearch, Application Insights, OpenTelemetry) can filter and aggregate. Interpolation would bake the values into a unique string and also format it even when the level is disabled.

Levels from lowest to highest: `Trace`, `Debug`, `Information`, `Warning`, `Error`, `Critical`. Configure minimum levels per category in configuration:

```json
"Logging": { "LogLevel": { "Default": "Information", "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning" } }
```

Pass exceptions as the first argument: `logger.LogError(ex, "Payment {Id} failed", id)` keeps the stack trace as structured data.

**Scopes** (`using (logger.BeginScope("Request {RequestId}", id))`) attach properties to every log in a block. For hot paths, the `[LoggerMessage]` source generator creates strongly typed, allocation-free logging methods.

Built-in providers write to console, debug and EventSource. Libraries like Serilog or the OpenTelemetry exporter plug into the same `ILogger` abstraction, so your code doesn't change when the destination does. Never log secrets, tokens or full personal data.
takeaways: Inject ILogger<T>; the type becomes the category
Use message templates with named placeholders, not interpolation
Configure minimum levels per category in Logging:LogLevel
Pass the exception as the first argument to LogError
pitfalls: Writing logger.LogInformation($"User {id}"), which loses structure and always formats the string.

quiz.q: Why prefer logger.LogInformation("User {Id}", id) over $"User {id}"?
options: Interpolated strings are not allowed in logs
Id is captured as a structured property and formatting is skipped when the level is disabled
quiz.explain: Message templates keep values as structured data and avoid formatting work for disabled levels.

concepts.name: OpenAPI documents
concepts.summary: Generate an OpenAPI description of your API with Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi and enrich it with endpoint metadata.
concepts.why: An OpenAPI document powers interactive docs, client generation and contract testing.
concepts.body:
ASP.NET Core can describe its endpoints as an **OpenAPI** document. Since .NET 9 this is built in through the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi` package (included in the `webapi` template); Swashbuckle is no longer part of the template.

```csharp
builder.Services.AddOpenApi();
app.MapOpenApi();        // serves /openapi/v1.json
```

In ASP.NET Core 10 the document uses **OpenAPI 3.1** by default, and you can also serve YAML (`app.MapOpenApi("/openapi/{documentName}.yaml")`).

The generator reads what it can from your code: routes, parameter types and binding sources, request bodies, and response types from `TypedResults` and `Results<...>` unions. Add more with metadata:

- `.WithName("GetTodo")` (operationId), `.WithSummary(...)`, `.WithDescription(...)`, `.WithTags("Todos")`.
- `.Produces<T>(201)`, `.ProducesProblem(404)` when the return type doesn't say it.
- XML doc comments are picked up when `GenerateDocumentationFile` is enabled (ASP.NET Core 10).
- Document and operation **transformers** customize the output, e.g. adding security schemes.

The package only produces JSON; for a UI, add Swagger UI (`Swashbuckle.AspNetCore.SwaggerUI`) or Scalar (`Scalar.AspNetCore`) pointing at the document, usually only in Development.

Treat the document as a contract: generate typed clients from it (NSwag, Kiota, openapi-generator) and diff it in CI to catch breaking changes.
takeaways: AddOpenApi + MapOpenApi serve /openapi/v1.json
TypedResults and Results<...> document responses automatically
Add names, summaries and tags with With* methods
UI tools like Swagger UI or Scalar are separate add-ons

quiz.q: Why do TypedResults help OpenAPI generation?
options: Their static types describe the possible responses and schemas
They are required for any document
quiz.explain: The generator inspects the declared return types, such as Results<Ok<Todo>, NotFound>, to list responses.

concepts.name: Integration testing with WebApplicationFactory
concepts.summary: Test the whole HTTP pipeline in memory with WebApplicationFactory, HttpClient and replaced services.
concepts.why: Integration tests catch routing, binding, DI and serialization bugs that unit tests miss.
concepts.body:
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing` provides `WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint>`, which boots your real app (its `Program`) on an in-memory **TestServer**. `factory.CreateClient()` returns an `HttpClient` wired to it: requests go through the full middleware pipeline, routing, binding and serialization, without opening a network port.

Setup:

- Create an xUnit project, add `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing`, and reference the web project.
- The test project needs access to `Program`. If the compiler can't see it, add `public partial class Program { }` at the end of the app's `Program.cs`.
- Use `IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>` to share one app instance across tests in a class.

Customize the app for tests with `WithWebHostBuilder`:

- `builder.UseEnvironment("Testing")` and `UseSetting("Key", "value")` for configuration.
- `ConfigureTestServices(services => ...)` to replace real dependencies (external APIs, clocks, email senders) with fakes. Remove the real registration or rely on the last registration winning.

For databases, prefer a real engine in a container (Testcontainers) or SQLite over the EF in-memory provider, which doesn't behave like a relational database.

Use `System.Net.Http.Json` helpers: `GetFromJsonAsync<T>`, `PostAsJsonAsync`, `ReadFromJsonAsync<T>`. Assert on status codes and response bodies, as an API client would.
takeaways: WebApplicationFactory<Program> hosts the real app in memory
CreateClient gives an HttpClient through the full pipeline
ConfigureTestServices swaps real dependencies for fakes
Prefer a real database engine over the EF in-memory provider
pitfalls: Testing only handlers in isolation and missing binding, routing or serialization bugs.

quiz.q: What does WebApplicationFactory.CreateClient() talk to?
options: A real Kestrel server on a random port
An in-memory TestServer running the app's full pipeline
A mock that returns 200 for everything
quiz.explain: Requests are processed in-memory by TestServer through the app's middleware and endpoints.

concepts.name: Authentication with JWT and cookies
concepts.summary: Identify users with authentication schemes, validate JWT bearer tokens and read claims from the user principal.
concepts.why: Almost every API must know who is calling before deciding what they may do.
concepts.body:
**Authentication** answers "who is this?". It's provided by **schemes** registered with `builder.Services.AddAuthentication(...)` and run by `app.UseAuthentication()` (WebApplication adds it automatically when auth services are registered). A successful scheme produces a `ClaimsPrincipal` available as `HttpContext.User` or a `ClaimsPrincipal` handler parameter.

Common schemes:

- **JWT bearer** (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer`) for APIs: clients send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. With an identity provider (Entra ID, Auth0, Keycloak), set `Authority` and `Audience`; the middleware downloads signing keys from the provider's OpenID metadata and validates signature, issuer, audience and lifetime.
- **Cookies** for server-rendered web apps; usually combined with **OpenID Connect** to sign in through an external provider.
- ASP.NET Core Identity and its API endpoints (`MapIdentityApi`) when you store users yourself.

A **claim** is a key/value statement about the user (`sub`, `email`, `role`). Read them with `user.FindFirst("sub")?.Value` or `user.Identity?.Name`. Avoid inventing your own token formats or crypto.

Authentication alone doesn't block anything: an anonymous request simply has an unauthenticated user. Blocking is the job of **authorization** (next lesson), which returns **401** (challenge: not authenticated) or **403** (forbid: authenticated but not allowed).

For local development, `dotnet user-jwts create` issues test tokens that the JwtBearer handler accepts.
takeaways: Authentication schemes turn credentials into a ClaimsPrincipal
JwtBearer validates signature, issuer, audience and expiry
Use cookies + OIDC for browser apps, bearer tokens for APIs
401 means not authenticated, 403 means not allowed
pitfalls: Disabling token validation parameters (issuer, audience, lifetime) to 'make it work'.

quiz.q: An endpoint requires authorization and the request has no token. What status is returned?
quiz.explain: No authenticated user means the scheme issues a challenge, which is a 401.

concepts.name: Authorization policies
concepts.summary: Control access with RequireAuthorization, roles, claims-based policies and resource-based checks.
concepts.why: Fine-grained, centralized access rules prevent the most damaging class of API bugs.
concepts.body:
**Authorization** decides whether the authenticated user may perform an action. Apply it to endpoints with `.RequireAuthorization()` (minimal APIs), `[Authorize]` (controllers), or to whole route groups. `.AllowAnonymous()` / `[AllowAnonymous]` opt out.

**Policies** name a set of requirements and keep rules in one place:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .AddPolicy("Admin", p => p.RequireRole("admin"))
    .AddPolicy("CanWrite", p => p.RequireClaim("scope", "todos.write"));
```

Use them with `.RequireAuthorization("CanWrite")`. Policy building blocks: `RequireAuthenticatedUser`, `RequireRole`, `RequireClaim`, `RequireAssertion(ctx => ...)` for inline logic, and custom `IAuthorizationRequirement` + `AuthorizationHandler<T>` classes for rules that need services (database lookups, time of day).

Set a **fallback policy** (`SetFallbackPolicy(...RequireAuthenticatedUser()...)`) to make every endpoint require login unless it explicitly allows anonymous access; this is safer than remembering to protect each new endpoint.

**Resource-based authorization** handles "may this user edit *this* document?". Load the resource, then call `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, document, "CanEdit")` with a handler that compares e.g. the owner id to the user's id. Return `Forbid()` when it fails.

Test authorization rules with integration tests for both allowed and denied cases.
takeaways: RequireAuthorization / [Authorize] apply policies to endpoints and groups
Define named policies once with roles, claims or assertions
A fallback policy protects endpoints by default
Use IAuthorizationService for per-resource checks
pitfalls: Checking roles with if statements scattered across handlers instead of named policies.

quiz.q: What does a fallback policy requiring an authenticated user achieve?
options: Endpoints without explicit authorization metadata still require login
quiz.explain: The fallback applies whenever an endpoint specifies no authorization, making protection the default.

concepts.name: Background services
concepts.summary: Run long-lived work with BackgroundService, timers and queues, using scoped services safely and stopping gracefully.
concepts.why: Queues, schedulers and cache warmers are part of most real services and must behave on shutdown.
concepts.body:
A **hosted service** runs alongside the web server for the app's lifetime. Derive from `BackgroundService` and implement `ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)`, then register it with `builder.Services.AddHostedService<T>()`.

```csharp
protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1));
    while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(ct)) { ... }
}
```

Key points:

- `stoppingToken` is canceled when the app shuts down. Pass it to every await so shutdown is quick; the host waits up to `HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout` (30 seconds by default).
- Hosted services are **singletons**. To use scoped services like a `DbContext`, inject `IServiceScopeFactory` and create a scope per unit of work: `using var scope = factory.CreateScope();`.
- Catch and log exceptions inside the loop. Since .NET 6, an unhandled exception in `ExecuteAsync` stops the whole host by default (`BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior.StopHost`).
- `PeriodicTimer` doesn't overlap ticks, unlike `System.Threading.Timer`.

For in-process work queues, combine a `Channel<T>` registered as a singleton: endpoints write work items and return 202 Accepted, and the background service reads them. Remember that in-memory queues are lost on restart; for durable jobs use a message broker or a library such as Hangfire or Quartz.NET.

When running multiple instances, every instance runs its hosted services, so scheduled jobs may need a distributed lock.
takeaways: BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync runs for the app's lifetime
Honor stoppingToken for fast, graceful shutdown
Create a scope per unit of work to use scoped services
Catch exceptions in the loop; unhandled ones stop the host
pitfalls: Injecting a DbContext directly into a hosted service constructor (a captive scoped dependency).

quiz.q: How should a BackgroundService use a scoped DbContext?
options: Create a scope with IServiceScopeFactory for each unit of work
quiz.explain: Hosted services are singletons, so scoped services must be resolved from a scope created per unit of work.

concepts.name: Route groups and endpoint filters
concepts.summary: Organize minimal APIs with MapGroup and add cross-cutting logic per endpoint with endpoint filters.
concepts.why: Groups and filters keep larger minimal API apps structured without repeating auth, prefixes and checks.
concepts.body:
**Route groups** share a prefix and conventions among endpoints:

```csharp
var todos = app.MapGroup("/api/todos").WithTags("Todos").RequireAuthorization();
todos.MapGet("/", GetAll);
todos.MapGet("/{id:int}", GetById);
```

Anything you can apply to one endpoint (authorization, rate limiting, caching, OpenAPI metadata, filters) can be applied to a group, and groups can be nested. A common structure is one static class per feature with a `MapTodoEndpoints(this IEndpointRouteBuilder app)` extension method that creates the group, keeping `Program.cs` tiny.

**Endpoint filters** run around a minimal API handler, after binding, much like MVC action filters:

```csharp
.AddEndpointFilter(async (ctx, next) => { /* before */ var result = await next(ctx); /* after */ return result; })
```

`ctx.Arguments` / `ctx.GetArgument<T>(index)` give access to the bound parameters, and `ctx.HttpContext` to everything else. Return a result early to short-circuit (for example a validation problem), or call `next` and transform its result.

Filters vs middleware: middleware sees every request but knows nothing about the endpoint's parameters; filters run only for the endpoints they're attached to and see typed arguments. Use filters for argument validation, auditing specific operations or wrapping responses; use middleware for global concerns.

Filters added to a group run for all its endpoints, in the order they're added (outer first). Reusable filters implement `IEndpointFilter`.
takeaways: MapGroup shares prefixes and conventions (auth, tags, filters)
Organize features as extension methods that map their own group
Endpoint filters see bound arguments and can short-circuit
Use middleware for global concerns, filters for endpoint-specific ones

quiz.q: What can an endpoint filter do that middleware cannot easily do?
options: Access the handler's bound, typed arguments
quiz.explain: Filters run after parameter binding and get the handler's arguments through the context.

concepts.name: Caching and rate limiting
concepts.summary: Speed up and protect APIs with output caching, HybridCache and the built-in rate limiting middleware.
concepts.why: Caching cuts latency and database load; rate limits protect your service from abuse and overload.
concepts.body:
**Output caching** stores whole responses on the server. Register `AddOutputCache()`, add `app.UseOutputCache()`, and mark endpoints with `.CacheOutput(p => p.Expire(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)))` or named policies. Vary by query, header or route values, and **evict by tag** (`IOutputCacheStore.EvictByTagAsync("todos")`) when data changes. Only GET/HEAD 200 responses for anonymous requests are cached by default.

**Data caching** caches values inside your code:

- `IMemoryCache`: in-process, fast, lost on restart, not shared between instances.
- `IDistributedCache` (Redis, SQL Server): shared, but you serialize bytes yourself.
- `HybridCache` (`Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Hybrid`, .NET 9+): combines an in-memory layer with an optional distributed one, handles serialization, and prevents **cache stampedes**: concurrent misses for one key run the factory only once. `await cache.GetOrCreateAsync(key, async ct => await LoadAsync(ct))`.

**Rate limiting** (`AddRateLimiter` + `app.UseRateLimiter()`) rejects excess requests, by default with 503; set `RejectionStatusCode = 429`. Algorithms: fixed window, sliding window, token bucket and concurrency limiters. Apply them with `.RequireRateLimiting("policy")` and partition by user or client IP so one client can't exhaust others' quota.

In-process limits apply per instance; behind a load balancer with many instances, enforce global limits at the gateway too.
takeaways: Output caching stores full responses; evict by tag on changes
HybridCache adds two-level caching and stampede protection
Rate limiters reject excess load; set 429 as the status code
Partition limits per user or IP
pitfalls: Output-caching endpoints whose responses depend on the authenticated user.

quiz.q: What status does the rate limiting middleware return for rejected requests unless configured otherwise?
quiz.explain: The default RejectionStatusCode is 503, so most apps set it to 429 explicitly.

concepts.name: Kestrel, proxies and deployment
concepts.summary: Configure Kestrel endpoints, limits and protocols, run behind reverse proxies with forwarded headers, and ship containers.
concepts.why: Production incidents often come from hosting details: wrong client IPs, HTTPS loops, limits and shutdowns.
concepts.body:
**Kestrel** is an async, event-driven server built on `System.IO.Pipelines`. It supports HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (QUIC), and TLS. Configure it in code (`builder.WebHost.ConfigureKestrel`) or in configuration under `Kestrel:Endpoints`; set URLs with `ASPNETCORE_URLS` or `ASPNETCORE_HTTP_PORTS` (container images default to port 8080).

Important **limits** (`KestrelServerLimits`): `MaxRequestBodySize` (about 28.6 MB default), `MaxConcurrentConnections`, request header limits, `KeepAliveTimeout`, and minimum data rates that defend against slow clients.

Behind a **reverse proxy** or load balancer (Nginx, YARP, Azure Front Door, Kubernetes ingress), the app sees the proxy's IP and plain HTTP. Use the **forwarded headers** middleware early in the pipeline so `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` update `RemoteIpAddress` and `Request.Scheme`. Only trust known proxies/networks (`KnownProxies`, `KnownIPNetworks`), otherwise clients can spoof their IP. Without this, `UseHttpsRedirection` can cause redirect loops and generated links use `http`.

**Graceful shutdown**: on SIGTERM the host stops accepting connections, lets in-flight requests finish, and stops hosted services, within `ShutdownTimeout`. Make sure your orchestrator's grace period is longer.

**Containers**: `dotnet publish /t:PublishContainer` builds an OCI image without a Dockerfile, using the official images, which run as a non-root user by default. Chiseled (distroless) base images reduce size and attack surface.
takeaways: Kestrel limits protect against oversized and slow requests
UseForwardedHeaders first, trusting only known proxy networks
Graceful shutdown drains requests within ShutdownTimeout
dotnet publish can build non-root container images directly
pitfalls: Trusting X-Forwarded-For from any source, letting clients fake their IP address.

quiz.q: Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, why does UseHttpsRedirection loop without forwarded headers?
options: The app sees every request as plain http and keeps redirecting
quiz.explain: Without X-Forwarded-Proto processing, Request.Scheme is http even for HTTPS clients.

concepts.name: Performance and Native AOT
concepts.summary: Make APIs fast and lean with async I/O, IHttpClientFactory, JSON source generation, CreateSlimBuilder and Native AOT.
concepts.why: Throughput, memory and cold start directly drive hosting costs and user-perceived latency.
concepts.body:
ASP.NET Core is among the fastest mainstream frameworks, but app code usually dominates. The main levers:

- **Never block** on async code (`.Result`, `.Wait()`, synchronous I/O). Blocking starves the thread pool and causes latency spikes under load ("thread pool starvation"). Synchronous body reads are disallowed by default for this reason.
- Use **IHttpClientFactory** (`AddHttpClient<T>`) for outbound calls: pooled handlers, DNS refresh, and resilience via `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience` (`AddStandardResilienceHandler`).
- **Stream** large responses (`IAsyncEnumerable<T>` is serialized as it's produced) instead of buffering whole lists.
- Reduce allocations in hot paths; check with `dotnet-counters` (allocation rate, GC, thread pool queue length) and `dotnet-trace`.
- Paginate and project database queries; most "slow API" problems are queries.

**Native AOT** compiles the app to a native executable: startup in tens of milliseconds and much lower memory, great for serverless and dense container hosting. It's supported for minimal APIs, gRPC and worker services, not MVC or Razor. Start with `dotnet new webapiaot` or set `<PublishAot>true</PublishAot>`, use `WebApplication.CreateSlimBuilder` (fewer default features), and register a **JSON source-generated context** so serialization needs no reflection. The **Request Delegate Generator** turns your `Map*` handlers into compile-time code automatically when AOT is enabled.

Fix every AOT/trim warning: they predict runtime failures.
takeaways: Blocking on async code causes thread pool starvation under load
Use IHttpClientFactory and stream large responses
Native AOT works with minimal APIs: CreateSlimBuilder + JSON source generation
Treat trim and AOT warnings as errors
pitfalls: Calling .Result on HttpClient calls inside request handlers, which looks fine in tests and collapses under load.

quiz.q: Why does Native AOT need a JsonSerializerContext?
options: Reflection-based serialization isn't available, so serialization code must be generated at compile time
Because AOT apps can't return JSON otherwise at all, even with source generation
quiz.explain: Source-generated contexts provide the type metadata that reflection would otherwise discover at runtime.

concepts.name: Health checks and observability
concepts.summary: Expose health endpoints and instrument the app with OpenTelemetry traces, metrics and logs.
concepts.why: You can't operate what you can't see: orchestrators need health signals and engineers need traces and metrics.
concepts.body:
**Health checks** tell load balancers and orchestrators whether to send traffic. Register checks with `builder.Services.AddHealthChecks().AddCheck<DbCheck>("db", tags: ["ready"])` and expose them with `app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz")`. Separate **liveness** (is the process responsive? keep it trivial) from **readiness** (can it serve traffic: database, dependencies) using tag predicates, so a database blip doesn't make Kubernetes restart every pod.

**Observability** in .NET is built on standard APIs:

- **Tracing** via `System.Diagnostics.Activity`. ASP.NET Core, HttpClient and many libraries create activities for incoming and outgoing requests, propagating W3C `traceparent` headers across services. Create your own with an `ActivitySource`.
- **Metrics** via `System.Diagnostics.Metrics.Meter` (counters, histograms, up-down counters). ASP.NET Core publishes built-in meters such as `http.server.request.duration` and Kestrel connection metrics.
- **Logs** via `ILogger`, correlated with the current trace id.

The **OpenTelemetry** .NET SDK (`OpenTelemetry.Extensions.Hosting`) collects all three and exports them over OTLP to backends like Prometheus/Grafana, Jaeger, Azure Monitor or Datadog: `AddOpenTelemetry().WithTracing(...).WithMetrics(...).UseOtlpExporter()`. .NET Aspire wires this up by default.

For live diagnostics without redeploying, use `dotnet-counters monitor`, `dotnet-trace collect` and `dotnet-dump`. Keep metric tag cardinality low: never tag with user ids or raw URLs.
takeaways: Separate liveness from readiness health checks
Traces use Activity/ActivitySource, metrics use Meter
OpenTelemetry collects and exports traces, metrics and logs over OTLP
Keep metric tag cardinality low
pitfalls: Making the liveness probe depend on the database, so a DB outage restarts every instance.

quiz.q: Why should a liveness probe usually not check the database?
options: A database outage would restart all healthy app instances without fixing anything
It is too slow to compile
quiz.explain: Liveness failures trigger restarts; dependency problems belong in readiness, which only stops traffic.
